title: People are addicted
author: Saytron3030
selftext:
OK gotcha headline over. People are addicted to CREATING THINGS they always have been. It is what makes us innately human.

What I have noticed with this AI game Dev is now people actually feel like it's possible with all the constraints of the modern world. Time has always been a luxury and skills take 1000s of hours to gain. Now creation is at the tips of our fingers.

We should give a break to people making clones of other games, being creative is hard, they haven't had much practice.

We will all get better and I think more accessibility to Creation is a good thing.

comments.author: guigouz
comments.body: Just because you can build fast doesn't mean you should build just for the sake of it.

replies.author: lorean_victor
replies.body:
why not? build, change a bit maybe, learn how things work, etc.

the fact that this type of low effort rapid fire building clutters up our current discovery and distribution channels is due the shortcomings of those channels. they are not built to handle this load and help people find stuff they’d like without getting bogged down.

replies.author: guigouz
replies.body:
As long as you have a proper spec and know what you want to build, that's fine. I'm just tired of people putting Astra/Fable to "build a <x> clone" and publishing it with no real goal.

You should put some thought and care into what you build.

replies.author: lorean_victor
replies.body: again why not? I agree that such clones shouldn’t get a lot of exposure, but again, the issue right now is that we can’t distinguish those from ones with a little more effort put into them.

replies.author: guigouz
replies.body: Maybe if whoever is willing to build something, stops for 30 seconds to consider "what am I building? why am I building this?" they'll have more chance to build an actually interesting game.

replies.author: lorean_victor
replies.body: it’s interesting for them. the fact that they can do it even. why should it bother you and me?

replies.author: guigouz
replies.body:
Not necessarily, most of those will never see a second release because the creator didn't care enough from the start. I've seen it multiple times while helping people with their projects.

I'm not telling anyone not to build, but to make it worth it. Just by spending time discussing the mechanics with your agent until you get a proper spec is already a major win (think about how people had to build full game design documents and really think about each step of the project when code was not cheap).

replies.author: Sector62f
replies.body: The answer that these channels will bring will eventually be to make everything (uploading a game and marketing it) way more expensive. I don't see it as a good thing.

replies.author: Saytron3030
replies.body: Missed the point entirely. Would you say you shouldn't make art for the sake of it or build a chair? It's a human thing to do and now Games are like widdling

replies.author: guigouz
replies.body: I think it depends on how much effort you're putting in it - if anyone can create anything, what differentiates your creations? You should have some respect for what you're building.

replies.author: blackskies69
replies.body: I disagree. Building fast exposes a lot of short comings and helps teaches the importance of iteration in game design. I can build a prototype in an hour, play it, test it, and find that its not enough. Some people are just too new to decide if their idea is good or not so they share in hopes for feed back. I don't see anything wrong with that. I think the bigger issue is we don't have a way to effectively sort through it yet. I love playing the slop games because they teach me what to avoid or what to do in my own games. I wish we had a system similar to what the AI RP community does with cards honestly. It would help with sorting everything so people can avoid seeing the low quality content that annoys them so much. While still allowing others to sate their curiosity.

replies.author: guigouz
replies.body:
If you have a vision and know what you want to build, that is indeed great, but in reality what we're seeing is a lot of people starting projects without even considering that it will have a second iteration.

A little bit of planning before building whatever increases the chances of making it worth maintaining in the long term.

replies.author: blackskies69
replies.body: And people learn from those failures all the same. They see a concept proven but not fleshed out and understand the difference thanks to critical peer review. There is a lot of bad information floating around social media pushing people to try and make a game with AI. Unfortunately there is no central authority for them to look towards for learning the process, so they have to fail first and learn. This won't always be the case. During the 90's there were a plethora of bad games being released as the hobby took over. It wasn't until there were experts for new people to lean on to help learn the process as it was being developed. This is the same scenario, the experts haven't been defined yet, and people really don't even know what they want to build yet. AI is going to enable a lot more mechanics and features in games we can't anticipate. We just need to define the standards, but before we can do that we need to learn what falls beneath it.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body: Why not? If you have never done it before, it's fun!

replies.author: guigouz
replies.body: So you can actually finish it, not just build whatever, share and never touch the project again.

replies.author: Fuzzzy420
replies.body: Yeah but even before ai, really Finishing a game was a challenge and it still is.

comments.author: legend-of-alan
comments.body:
So in general, I agree on most of what you’re saying. Especially on the point of accessibility.

But I think this whole vibe coding thing making people think they can create games is addicting in the wrong sort of way. A lot of vibecoding shares characteristics with slot machine dynamics. One more turn of the AI or one more prompt — it might fix the thing you want and make your game better or it might generate garbage or create more problems that fixes. The key point is randomly distributed rewards and big dopamine hits. That’s gambling.

Worse so with games is that AI isn’t good enough to maintain these large systems. A lot of vibe coded games have the problem that the first iteration is one of the best and every subsequent iteration has diminishing returns. It’s the problem of painting over the walls instead of cleaning them properly and after five or six coats you’ve got a mess.

So in general, I’m glad that AI has made games so much more accessible, but my heart take right now is that it’s it’s a false God right now and people are using a lot more money than is justifiable.

At the current stage, I think hybrid tools are the best for AI game dev. They allow you some freedom to design what you want and AI shorten the lead time. But if you get full freedom, like trying to write something in unreal, or God forbid writing your own from the ground up, oh shit you’re going to have a really bad time

replies.author: caesium23
replies.body:
You have some legit points, but only talking about vibe coding leads you to overstate your conclusion: A lot of the Redditors in this sub, and basically all of the ones who seem remotely serious instead of just dropping the occasional ooh-shiny-look-what-I-one-shotted post, are doing actual AI-assisted development, not just "vibe coding."

In other words, if your point is "AI is a false god," I think you're focusing on the least useful way to use it and thus overstating your position, but if your point is "one shotting is a false god," then you're not wrong, but this is the most lukewarm take ever – I think someone repeats it in every fourth thread I read on here.

replies.author: legend-of-alan
replies.body:
Thanks for the correction there, and I think we agree more than not.

To clarify, My comment was not about oneshotting or about disparaging ai-assisted development for those who have strong fundamentals. It was actually more about dictating behavior and trying to iterate to a finished product without looking at code. The “lights off software factory” experiment didn’t work as well as we’d hoped, even within the software industry—Let alone non-developers using ai to abstract out the programming part of game dev.

So I don’t mean to conflate vibe coding and ai-assisted programming, but I’m new enough to the sub to not know what “most people” are doing, so I can only speak generally on patterns I’ve observed. Based on your comment, I misjudged the ratio of people on this sub.

replies.author: caesium23
replies.body: I've only been coming to this sub for a couple weeks, so I might not be the final word about what's most common either, but that's been my impression. I can definitely say that I've seen this sentiment expressed multiple times already in my short time here. But whether that makes it the majority opinion or just a vocal minority, I guess is hard to say.

comments.author: delicious_pubes
comments.body: People should make clones. It’s a great way to learn design. Clone then figure out why your game sucks when the original is fun. What people shouldn’t do is sell clones or see this as an easy way to make money.

replies.author: guigouz
replies.body: Make clones by asking "build a clone" or to actually understand how the original works?

replies.author: delicious_pubes
replies.body: Depends what you mean by understand how it works. If the goal is design then building a slop clone and iterating til it’s good (but scoped small) will be educational. If the goal is engineering then I wouldn’t approach it that way at all.

replies.author: WarmWombat
replies.body:
Let’s face it, you would only clone something if you lack the creative talent and vision to create your own idea. People only clone to capitalise on the ideas of others.   
With AI it is already hard to see how someone else did something. Not sure what the real education value is. You don’t have to clone something to learn how it works.

This sounds more like a poor excuse to create more slop.

replies.author: delicious_pubes
replies.body:
I don’t disagree with your skepticism. I have been a professional game designer in AAA and AA studios for a decade and I got started by cloning games from scratch just to learn. Trying to always invent new things and have an original vision without actually understanding how things work and play together is how you end up with scope creep and being the dreaded “ideas guy”.

AI is creating a huge gap between those who intrinsically want to learn and those who would rather offload their thinking, hit send to the dopamine machine, and have delusions of grandeur and riches when their brain takes credit for what the AI presented them.

But the statement that “people only clone to capitalize on the ideas of others” is insanely reductive and an oversimplification of creative work. Everything is derivative and people are often drawing inspiration from the same sources. There is a difference between cloning for learning and cloning because you’re a hack.

comments.author: Falendil
comments.body:
Making copies is not creating.

Puting your spin on a formula  is not the same thing as making a carbon copy of someone's else création.

comments.author: Sector62f
comments.body:
I disagree that more accessibility is a good thing. I like when things are being gatekept if the only gatekeeping is "are you willing to put in the hours to learn this ?".

But I acknowledge that it is a widely unpopular opinion, especially here.

replies.author: Sector62f
replies.body:
And I support AI-assisted game dev for the same reason. Slotbounds is a good game made with AI over the course of many months, and I have 0 problem with that. The guy spent the required time to get good at making a game.

My problem lies with the low quality AI games flooding Steam. I wish those could not go through the gate.

replies.body:
Other then the 100 dollar fee , there is no reasonable gate.

tbh people have far overblown the issue , if an indie dev slops out a game and puts it up on steam quickly , it gets buried near instantly.

thats why the prevailing advice at the moment is to have your steam page up and start marketing 6 months before release , if you gather a lot of wishlists and have a great launch , steam multiplies it by advertising your game on the frontpage , which makes it sell even more.


Some dude who prompted a game in 3 days and puts it up wont get that treatment

replies.author: Sector62f
replies.body:
More people doing this means more competition to get seen, even if your game is good.

It means that game dev will gradually shift towards giving an even more important share to marketing, both in terms of time and budget. 

I am living with my time and rolling with the punches, so I adapt to this new thing. But I wish it was not the case.

replies.author: CptFlamex
replies.body:
I understand , if it makes you feel any better this has been the case for the past decade , every year there are record numbers of new developers on steam and record number of games.

The good news is there are more gamers than ever , all you can do is focus on making your game the best it can be and trying to market it as best you can

replies.author: Time_Cat_5212
replies.body:
I think that most established activities gatekeep themselves on those terms by nature of the output, and we don't need a layer of people with attitudes about it to enforce that.

There's kind of a "bell curve meme" with creative work. An accomplished, professional designer isn't going to give a damn about newbies hacking it "the wrong way" like an amateur enthusiast might.

replies.author: caesium23
replies.body: You do know a bell curve is just... a real thing that exists in math, not something made up by meme culture... right?

replies.author: Time_Cat_5212
replies.body:
Duh. The meme expresses a specific pattern in which the extremes agree on a simple conclusion while the middle overcomplicates things.

In this case, instead of intelligence, the horizontal axis would be experience.

comments.author: Rolotine
comments.body:
Something I’ve noticed (which isn’t a bad thing) is that a lot of people who haven’t really ever engaged with creative spaces or put anything they’ve made out onto the internet are discovering what that process is like. I’ll give a brief example: I put fanfictions I write online and have for probably close to 2 decades now. Most wither on the vine; that’s fine, because I enjoyed writing them and wasn’t really looking to make money or generate a reader audience. They exist, maybe they get some views (most likely spiders or scraper bots that steal the free content to repost elsewhere), but that’s just how the ecosystem is. Sometimes I’d get a random positive comment, and very rarely I’d get a story that attracted enough attention to get several. And sometimes I’d get really nasty comments! There are people who just hate things and also actively search out content they hate; this is especially true if you produce anything that might hit the radar of the anti-LGBTQ crowd.

And the other side of the creative coin is needing to be able to filter feedback. Obviously you should engage with a hobby in the way that best protects your mental health and gives you the most enjoyment, but also if you want to improve at your craft you have to learn how to interpret critique. Some really negative awful comments may still have truth to them. Some really positive glowing comments might be completely worthless. And sometimes it doesn’t matter either way because you have a vision and that’s what you want to execute on. comments be damned. But you gotta have some system in mind.

I see a lot of people entering into creative spaces who haven’t built any of these mechanisms or strategies yet and sort of implode on impact. Traditionally if you were starting out, you would put out very clear amateur proof of concepts or short stories or little nuggets that were pieces of a larger chunk of a work. But now folks can dump an entire vibecoded project in one go, and post their steam page, and have a slick AI generated trailer, and each one of those things used to be an individual element you would expose to feedback and build up your expectations around. And I think some people who might have great ideas and who could build cool things might get burned because of that! It’s not so much gatekeeping but more like how entering spaces you are unfamiliar with is almost always going to produce friction, and I see way too many posts that are to the tune of ‘people should change to accommodate me’ rather than ‘I need to learn how to accommodate other people’. And I don’t have an ending to this ramble, I just hope people don’t get hurt because the creative process is being short-circuited now. Like you're gonna get push-back no matter what, and even stronger push back on things people don't like, and you have to learn to process that in a productive way or you'll suffer in the long run.

comments.author: ButterRecipe
comments.body: It is good in ways but the same thing is happening to game dev that happened to fine art with instagram that the market is flooded with mediocrity and it's still difficult to find the rare exceptional or novel games. I expect there to be an enormously flood of indie games in the next few years and that 99.99% of them will essentially be clones with a wrapper or slight twist. What I'm interested in seeing is what totally new systems/engines/ideas people can come up with once the ability to reach for what was impossible before has some time to digest.

comments.author: programmervsworld
comments.body: People should do what makes them happy and healthy and not make decisions based on comments in reddit. You totally should make anything you want.

comments.author: DeanRayGames
comments.body:
"Give them a break" might be going too far if you mean "don't criticize at all." If a person is asking for feedback and their game is slop, then they deserve honest feedback. If its a derivative clone of another game that doesn't add anything at all, and they share it and want feedback, that's a good criticism to give them. 

But your point about copying things to learn how to do it is absolutely100%. Even the great artists in history went through training that involved copying greats before them. The difference is that when you copy something, you do it as a training exercise, you don't try to claim it as your own work and try to profit off of it.
